name: Mother Ione
appearance: The Prior of Saint Ysolde's, in her seventies: small and very upright, white hair cropped close under a plain linen coif, a soft round face creased like a winter apple, and pale eyes that count everyone in a room in turn. Gentle in face and manner, with iron under it. In the warming room she has the one good chair by the fire and offers it to nobody.
last_seen_doing: In the court after Darrow gave his name at the bars and the Confessor thanked her for her candour, asking Darrow only whether the shoulder was hurt.
now: Prior of Saint Ysolde's, with Confessor Ivo Marrant camped on the lower terrace below her gate. She let him read his list at the bars, and when he held his paper out under the law of guests she kept him waiting for the bell as long as she could, then had the wicket opened; two grey cloaks came through it before Old Mercy rang, late, and she spoke the law of names. When Darrow gave his name at the bars and the House's story died at her gate, the Confessor thanked her for her candour. She did not reproach Darrow; she asked whether his shoulder was hurt.
story_so_far: When the grey cloaks were sighted on the Holloway, the news went first to Mother Ione. She called a council in the warming room off the cloister: Maelis, Sister Pell, Rae Thorne who had heard the list read, and Darrow, whose name is first on it. She asked how it was read, had the law of Old Mercy said aloud for the Captain, and asked Sister Pell whether she would ring it dawn and dusk for as long as the grey cloaks wait. The council broke with nothing decided aloud, and she called Darrow back to ask what she ought to know before she decides. At the next dawn bell she came to the foot of Darrow's cot: the winch-brothers had taken his far side of the mountain down to the valley, Old Mercy had not rung and would not, for nobody, and when the grey cloaks are at the bars he is to tell Wren when. In the hour before dusk she stood before the gate and let the Confessor read; she kept him waiting at the wicket for the bell as long as the law of guests allowed, and when his men came through and the bell rang late, she gave him the law's other half, that no name under it is taken down against its will. When Darrow gave his name at the bars, the Confessor thanked her for her candour, and she asked Darrow only whether the shoulder was hurt.

quote.text: While it rings, no name under it is taken down against its will. Would your men like to go back out the way they came?

known_facts.fact: By the time Wren Ashdown reached the infirmary hall with word of the grey cloaks on the Holloway, Mother Ione had been told.
She holds her council in the warming room off the cloister, has the one good chair by the fire, and offers it to nobody.

She asked Rae Thorne how the list was read, had Maelis give Darrow the law of Old Mercy, and asked Sister Pell whether she would ring it dawn and dusk for as long as the grey cloaks care to sit at the bottom.

She has not yet decided whether Old Mercy rings. She called Darrow back from the stair to ask what he would have her know first, and what the lay brothers should tell the valley when it asks who sleeps up here.
known_facts.evidence: Before I decide whether Old Mercy rings, is there anything you'd have me know?

known_facts.fact: She let the Captain ask to be sent down and the Mender answer him, then closed the council having heard them all: Sister Pell would hear from her before dusk, and the lay brothers would want to know what to say to the valley.
known_facts.evidence: you'll hear from me before dusk

known_facts.fact: She came up the hall on the last stroke of the dawn bell and waited at the foot of Darrow's cot until Benedek's lips stopped moving before she spoke.
At first light the winch-brothers went down with Darrow's story of the far side of the mountain, to tell it at the winch-house fire, so that the valley would have it by noon.
known_facts.evidence: with your far side of the mountain

known_facts.fact: She asked Darrow whether he told it for the House or for the river; he said the river had had enough of them.
Old Mercy did not ring at dusk after her council, nor at the next dawn, and she says it will not ring for nobody: a bell rung for nobody tells the valley there's somebody.
known_facts.evidence: A bell rung for nobody tells the valley there's somebody

known_facts.fact: When Darrow said the law was down, she said it had been since dusk and asked whether he had slept any worse for it; it comes back with the next ringing.
known_facts.evidence: Did you sleep any worse for it?

known_facts.fact: She asked Darrow, who reads a line before it moves, to tell Wren when, once the grey cloaks are at the bars; it was not a question, and he said he would.
She ordered nobody into the court; at the hour bell she asked whether the House would like to see who had climbed so far to read to it, and the House came.
She stood before the gate with Maelis a pace behind her shoulder; when the Confessor said she would forgive him if he read anyway, she asked, 'Would I stop you?'

She let the Confessor hold his paper out through the bars while the bell did not come; when he said he would hate to tell the bell-houses her House broke the law of guests to keep a courier standing in the cold, she asked the gate-ward whether they should take the Confessor's paper.
known_facts.evidence: shall we take the Confessor's paper?

known_facts.fact: When Old Mercy rang she told the Confessor, without moving and lowering her voice so the court leaned to hear, that while it rings no blade climbs the Steps or passes the gate, and the other half, which his order reads at every bell-house twice over: no name under it is taken down against its will.
known_facts.evidence: no name under it is taken down against its will

known_facts.fact: When Darrow gave his name at the bars and the Confessor thanked her for her candour, she did not look at the gate; she looked at Darrow and asked him whether the shoulder was hurt.
known_facts.evidence: She asked him whether the shoulder was hurt.

known_facts.fact: When Darrow offered to go down on the cage so the list would have nothing to climb for, she asked him how many names the next writ would carry once the House had given them one, and did not wait for him to count.
known_facts.evidence: how many will the next writ carry?

relationships.label: the Confessor who read his list at her gate
relationships.note: She let him read, made him wait at the wicket for the bell, and answered his men with the bell and the law of names; when the Captain gave his name, Marrant thanked her for her candour.
